children: Iron ore futures rose on Wednesday, as supply disruption in Brazil linked to El Niño provided short-term support even as weak steel mill profitability remained a drag.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
traded 0.56% higher at 715.5 yuan ($106.77) a metric ton, as of 0200 GMT.
The benchmark October iron ore <SZZFV6> on the Singapore Exchange was up 0.64% to $96.65 a ton.
Prices continued to stabilise after last week's sharp fall, with demand typically strengthening ahead of the Golden Week holiday in October, analysts from ANZ Research said in a note.
Supply disruption in Brazil linked to El Niño weather patterns is also providing short-term support to prices, the analysts said.

The blast furnace operating rate among 247 steel mills fell 0.8 percentage points week-on-week to 82.32% as of September 22, while capacity utilisation rose 0.5 percentage points to 89.23%, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
Weak steel mill profitability remained a drag.

Elevated coking coal prices continue to pressure steel mill margins, with coking coal climbing to $262 a ton on September 18, up 36.5% year-on-year, as safety inspections and mine suspensions in Shanxi curbed domestic supply, BMI analysts said in a report.
Prices continue to be weighed down by a strong supply outlook, softer confidence in China's steel demand prospects, and the ramp-up of the Simandou project in Guinea, the BMI analysts added.
Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE fell, with coking coal
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were mixed. Rebar
